To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
lipoteichoic acids (LTA) of group A strep- tococci are involved in adherence and colonization of these bacteria in the host.
the lipoteichoic acids of group A strepococci are involved in attachment of strepococcal cells to mucosal surfaces.
lipoteichoic acids of group A strep- tococci are spontaneously adsorbed onto erythrocytes and human epithelial cells by virtue of ester-linked fatty acid residues.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the cell membrane-binding properties of streptococccal LTA.
the role of LTA in the attachment of group A strepococci to epithelial cells.
the chemical and biological properties of LTA from group A strep.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the LTA molecule, as a whole, is the cell membrane-binding component of streptococcosis.

the LTA of group A strep. is composed of a lipid moiety, which contains ester-linked fatty acid(s) and glycerolphosphates, and a carbohydrate moiety, which is not involved in its RBC-sensitizer activity, but contains alanine.
the lipoteichoic acids (LTA) of the group A streptoccus (S. pyogenes) have a lipid moiety which is involved in the adsorption of the molecule to erythrocyte membranes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

LTA, which is a major cell wall component of group A strepococci, contains alanine, glycerolphosphate and esterified lipids, and that the latter two are involved in its cell membrane binding properties.
the group A streptcocal LTA has a structure similar to the LTA from Staphylococcus aureus.
the LTA is an amphiphilic molecule with hydrophilic (glycerolphosphate) and hydrophobic (fatty acid esters) domains, which spontaneously adsorbs to cell surfaces.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the LTA of streptococcosis is an important virulence factor and is responsible for the attachment and colonization of the bacteria in the human host.
LTA is a major component of the cell wall of group A strep and that it can bind to erythrocyte membranes and epithelial cells.

the LTA of group A strep, which we have shown is a potent adhesion, can be extracted from the cell membrane with phenol, and the extracted LTA can be separated into two fractions by ion exchange chromatography.
